The DPA of Cyprus fined the Cyprus electricity authority €5,000 for violations of Articles 5(1)(f), 24(1) and 32 GPDR for delivering a consent form containing personal data to the data subject's neighbour, resulting in an unauthorized disclosure of personal data to a third party.

The annual report describes a case in which a tip-off from the public led the fining office to obtain a search warrant for a pharmacy. The search found many documents containing health data (prescriptions with diagnoses, receipts, Covid test results) in large waste containers in a room accessible to unauthorised persons, despite shredders at the workstations. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 6,500 for the improper disposal, taking into account the pharmacy's cooperation and improved measures. For the unlawful video surveillance of the whole shop, including staff, no fine was imposed after the pharmacy complied with the authority's requirements.

The annual report of the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority describes a debt collection company that received a list of investor data from an employee of an insolvent firm. The data subjects did not know and had not agreed. The company used the list to offer the investors its services (filing insolvency claims and supporting the proceedings) without telling them where the data came from. The authority saw this as a breach of Art. 6(1) GDPR together with Art. 14(1) and (2) GDPR and found that the legitimate-interest basis did not apply. The fine was set so that it at least skimmed off the estimated revenue from the unlawful offer. The report gives no amount for this fine and says it has become final.

A hacker attacked an employee's business email account at a company, and applicants' email addresses leaked. The company did not notify the Bremen authority of the breach under Art. 33 GDPR. The authority learned of it through a complaint from an affected person and imposed a fine. The report does not state the amount for this case.

The Bremen data protection authority's 2022 annual report says it fined a supermarket company under Article 83 GDPR. A store detective had photographed a suspected shoplifter, without a legal basis, and passed the photo on via WhatsApp. The report does not give the amount of this fine or the articles breached. The WhatsApp transfer, which took place outside the EU, was counted as aggravating.

The Hamburg DPA's 2022 annual report describes a fine against an unnamed Hamburg logistics company. Employees had disposed of delivery lists containing subscribers' names, addresses and delivery notes in open public waste bins, and the company's disposal concept was inadequate. The authority found a breach of Art. 32(1) GDPR and imposed a fine, but the report gives no amount and calls it moderate. The company had a prior 2019 warning for a similar case, cooperated with the authority, and has lodged an objection, so the fine notice is not yet final.

In its 2022 annual report the Hamburg data protection authority describes a fine against a medical practice that also offered Covid tests. Staff left a rubbish sack with written positive and negative Covid-19 rapid test results of patients next to a public glass-recycling container, with no protection against third parties seeing them. The authority took the pandemic workload into account, but because health data was handled carelessly and many people were affected it did not drop the administrative offence proceedings. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000, which the practice accepted.

In its 2022 annual report the Hamburg data protection authority describes several fine proceedings against Covid-19 test centres. In one case a test centre emailed tested people an unencrypted link to their test result. The file name in the link was the person's surname, so anyone could read other people's results by swapping the name, in at least 189 cases. The authority found a breach of the duty to secure personal (health) data with suitable technical and organisational measures under Art. 32(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 2,700. The report does not name the test centre or give a date for the fine.

The Hamburg data protection authority's 2022 annual report describes several fines against Covid-19 test centers. In the case matching this entry, a test center scanned the front and back of its tested customers' identity cards and kept them on an external hard drive, to protect itself against queries from the statutory health insurance physicians' association. The authority found no legal obligation covering this storage beyond the data listed in the Coronavirus Test Ordinance, and the center did not cooperate constructively to end the unlawful practice. It imposed a fine of around EUR 1,400. The report does not name the center or give a decision date.

In the 2022 annual report the Hessian data protection commissioner describes a fine proceeding against a company that runs several Covid test centres, mainly in the Rhine-Main area. The company sent an email to about 100 people with the addresses visible in an open distribution list, and took no further action after a recipient pointed this out the same day. It was fined EUR 10,000 for the unlawful disclosure of the addresses (Art. 6(1) GDPR) and EUR 6,400 for failing to document the data breach (Art. 33(5) with 33(1) GDPR), EUR 16,400 in total. The fines were set using an estimate of the company's prior-year turnover and the Art. 83(2) criteria. The authority took into account the company's cooperation, its insight, the appointment of a data protection officer and the absence of earlier known violations. The company did not appeal.

The 2022 annual report of the Hessian data protection authority describes a fine against the operator of a Covid test centre in Hesse. An employee took a label from the bin, wrote the centre's e-mail address on it and stuck it on the plexiglass window, but the label still showed a customer's personal data such as name and test time. The data was therefore visible to an unlimited group of people. The authority found breaches of the principles of lawfulness and integrity/confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(a) and (f)) and of Art. 6(1) GDPR, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,800. The operator showed insight and paid the fine.

In its 2022 annual report the Hessian data protection commissioner describes fining a police officer a total of EUR 7,380 plus costs. The officer had used various police databases, or databases available to the police, for queries for his own purposes. The extent was exceptional: several hundred queries over three years. The report says the decision was not yet final. The report does not name the GDPR articles for this case.

The Hessian data protection commissioner's 2022 annual report describes a fine proceeding against a female police employee. She ran several queries in the residents' register (EWO) about her ex-husband's new partner, among other things to find out where her ex-husband was staying with their children. Such queries are one of the 'employee excess' cases, where staff access data for private motives. The proceeding ended with a fine notice of EUR 300, which was not contested and was paid. The report does not name the articles of the GDPR infringed in this case.

The 51st annual report of the Hessian data protection commissioner (reporting year 2022) describes in its fines chapter how the authority sanctioned misuse of police systems by officers for private reasons. In one case a police officer repeatedly looked up a female colleague in the EWO residents' register, although a block on disclosing her information was registered. The search parameters returned over 300 hits, so a lot of third-party data was disclosed. The commissioner imposed a fine of EUR 800 on the officer, and the fine decision is already final. The report gives no day for the decision and cites no GDPR articles for this fine.

The Brandenburg data protection authority's 2022 annual report describes a fine against the operator of an outdoor swimming pool. In the summer of 2021 visitors had to give, on Covid contact-tracing forms, their names, phone number, place of residence and the date and time of their stay, although the applicable regulation required only names, a phone number or e-mail address, and the date and time of stay. About 4,700 records were collected. Following a complaint, the authority found that collecting the place of residence was not necessary for the legal obligation and imposed a fine in the five-figure range, which the operator accepted. The report gives no exact amount.

The Brandenburg authority's annual report for 2022 describes a case against a district branch of an aid and welfare organisation. The branch reported a personal data breach after a hacker attack on its website, where patient transport records including health data were entered. The authority found that the branch did not take adequate technical and organisational measures. It also left a security gap open on a second, duplicate website for about three months despite knowing of it. The authority imposed a fine in the five-figure range, with no exact amount given, and the branch accepted it.

In a case the report calls serious, a sports photographer published over 16,000 photos of minors in swimwear, taken at a swimming competition, on a freely accessible website for sale. The company could not prove valid consent from the minors or their parents, and its press privilege argument failed because the photos were not edited journalistically and their further use was not limited to journalistic purposes. The authority imposed a fine by penalty notice, which was not yet final at the time of the report. The report gives no amount and no article numbers for this case.

The 2022 annual report of the Lower Saxony data protection authority describes a case in which a company's e-mail newsletter system did not allow unsubscribing for a relevant period. Because the company sent newsletters frequently, some data subjects received many unwanted e-mails. Unsubscribe requests made via customer service also failed, so objections to advertising were not respected. In at least one case a requested access reply was not given either. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 50,000, which the company accepted. The report does not name the company or give the article numbers for this case.

In its 2022 annual report the Lower Saxony data protection authority describes a fine of EUR 8,900 on a company that left a customer database with tens of thousands of entries reachable on the internet. The only protection was a very long, random-looking web address, with no username or password, and the address was usually requested unencrypted, so it could easily fall into the wrong hands. The authority took into account special circumstances of the case, namely that the business was partly being given up. The fine was accepted. The report does not name the company or the date of the decision.

In the annual report the Lower Saxony data protection commissioner describes a case in which a man was checked by the police after teenage girls reported that he was following and photographing them. His smartphone held several photographs of the girls taken in public space. The authority weighed the interests involved and stressed the special protection owed to children and young people. It imposed a fine of EUR 500, which the man accepted.

A credit reporting agency stored 27 wrong addresses and 13 wrong birth dates about one complainant for more than two years. It then answered the complainant's access request wrongly, first as a negative answer, and more than three months late. The authority fined the operator two times, a total of EUR 46,500, because it had already been warned several times for similar breaches. The report gives no separate amount per fine and no decision date.

The authority ran a fine procedure against a company's data protection officer after he posted a photo of a person from a bachelor party in the company's internal WhatsApp group, without that person's consent. The authority held that the household exemption did not apply, because the group was used for both private and business communication, and that no legal basis under Art. 6(1)(f) existed. A fine in the three-digit range was imposed, and the report says it is now final. The report gives no exact amount.

The Croatian data protection agency, acting ex officio, found that a bank published the national ID number (OIB) and home address of prize-game winners on its website, which exceeded what was necessary and lacked a legal basis. It found violations of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and issued a formal reprimand (službena opomena) and a prohibition on the excessive publication, with no fine.

Following several complaints, the CNIL carried out an online inspection of two websites run by the Google group and found that users could not refuse cookies as simply as they could accept them. The restricted committee found a breach of Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (the ePrivacy cookie rule) by both companies. It fined Google LLC (the US company) EUR 90 million and Google Ireland Limited (the Irish company) EUR 60 million, EUR 150 million in total. The published decision masks both companies' names; the CNIL's own press release names them. It also ordered both to change how consent is collected from users in France, with a daily penalty of EUR 100,000 after three months, and ordered the decision to be published, naming the companies for two years. The committee noted the very large number of people concerned, the profits drawn from advertising, and that the companies had been recently sanctioned for related cookie failings.

Following four complaints, the CNIL carried out an online inspection of the facebook.com website in April 2021. It found that the Irish company did not give users in France a way to refuse cookies as simply as to accept them, which undermines freedom of consent under Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (the ePrivacy cookie rule). The CNIL rejected the argument that the Irish authority was competent under the one-stop-shop mechanism. It fined Facebook Ireland Limited EUR 60 million, ordered it to provide an equally simple means of refusal, with a penalty of EUR 100,000 per day after three months, and ordered the decision to be published, naming the company for two years. The published decision masks the company's name; the CNIL's own press release names it, and the Conseil d'État order of 5 December 2022 on the challenge to this decision names the same company under its new name, Meta Platforms Ireland Limited.

The Greek DPA examined two complaints about promotional telephone calls (one live-agent call and one automated call) telling recipients they had won a prize, with a premium-rate number to call back for 'discount gift vouchers'. The calls came from numbers held by PLUS REAL ADVERTISMENT, which claimed participants had consented by entering their details in its promotions. The Authority found infringements of Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 (unsolicited communications), noting the controller aimed at financial gain, had no complaint-handling procedure and did not obtain valid consents. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 25,000.

Over several years the Authority received ten complaints about automated promotional calls (and one SMS) offering prizes or supermarket vouchers, without identifying the company on whose behalf they were made. The numbers were traced to INCOSER, which claimed participants had signed up themselves and consented. The Authority found breaches of the information duties in Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 (unsolicited calls, including to numbers on the opt-out register). It imposed a fine of EUR 30,000, noting the company profited financially, had no complaints procedure, did not respond in time to the Authority and was ignorant of the legal framework, but is now inactive.

A data subject complained that an online media publication had published his name and the fee he received for a project, together with a table of payments from an EU-funded project. The Croatian DPA found that the publication was lawful under the Media Act and the public interest in how public funds are spent, that the disclosed data were limited to what was necessary, and that there was a legal basis under Article 6. It rejected the request as unfounded, and no fine was imposed.

The CNIL investigated a furniture retailer selling online and in store in several EU countries. It found that the company had no retention periods for customer and prospect data and kept data for excessive periods, gave incomplete information to individuals, and had breaches concerning erasure requests, processor contracts and security. The CNIL initially planned only an order, but the Berlin authority raised a relevant and reasoned objection asking for a fine. The Restricted Committee found the breaches of Articles 5(1)(e), 13, 17, 28 and 32 GDPR established and imposed a fine of EUR 120,000. It imposed no injunction because the company had brought itself into compliance during the proceedings.

A citizen trying to log in to the Ministry of Tourism's 'Tourism for All' platform with tax credentials was shown another person's application data, including tax and social security numbers, contact details and disability fields. The Ministry did not notify the breach to the Authority, and its listed DPO email address was inactive because no DPO had been designated at the time. The Authority found breaches of Articles 13, 32, 33 and 37 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 75,000 on the Ministry.

The CNIL restricted committee fined a payment institution (the published decision withholds its name; the name on this page comes from the CNIL press release) EUR 180,000. In 2015 the company copied debtor data into a test server that stayed open on the internet after a fraud-research project ended in 2016. The breach, notified in February 2020, affected about 12 million debtors, with identity, contact and bank identifiers (BIC/IBAN). The committee also found that the company's contracts with its sub-processors lacked the Article 28(3) clauses, and that its checks on them were insufficient. It found failings under Articles 28(3) and (4), 32 and 34, and ordered publication of the decision with the company's name removed after two years.

The CNIL restricted committee fined a mobile phone operator EUR 300,000 for breaches of GDPR articles 12, 15, 21, 25 and 32. The case began with 19 complaints, mainly about difficulties exercising access and opposition rights, and it was followed by on-site and desk inspections. The committee found failures to answer an access request, to honour opposition requests, privacy-by-design shortcomings, and a security failure in sending customers' passwords by unencrypted email. It also ordered publication of the decision, naming the company for two years, but did not impose the proposed compliance injunction because the company had already taken compliance measures.
The Austrian DPA held that the use of Google Analytics by an Austrian website provider led to transfers of personal data to Google LLC in the U.S. in violation of Chapter V. of the GDPR.

The Danish DPA examined direct mail letters the Conservative People's Party sent to selected households before the 2019 European Parliament and Danish general elections. The party obtained names and addresses of recipients via the data distributor Geomatic and did not inform the recipients. The DPA found the processing lawful under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, but rejected the party's argument that the Article 14(5)(c) exemption applied and issued a reprimand for failing to meet the Article 14 information duty. No fine was imposed.

The Portuguese DPA issued a €1,250,000 fine against the Lisbon Municipality for sharing personal and sensitive data of protestors with third parties, including the embassies and foreign ministers of the countries targeted by the protests.

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority fined the transport company T. Stene Transport AS NOK 40,000 for unlawfully running a credit check on a sole proprietorship. The authority says credit information on a sole proprietorship is personal data, because the owner is directly identified with the business and it is tied to the owner's private finances. The company therefore needed a legal basis for the check. It was also ordered to set up routines for when it may obtain credit checks, even though it had not used the credit tool before and did not run checks regularly.

The DPA held that neither EU law or national law require that the controller replies to an access request containing "criminal data" or “sensitive data” delivering the information by hand. An answer can be given by electronic means, especially if the data subject asked so.

The Italian DPA investigated Enel Energia after many complaints and reports about unsolicited telemarketing calls, including to numbers on the opposition register and prerecorded calls, plus problems with handling data subject rights. It found 14 violations covering accountability and privacy by design, data accuracy, transparency, objection rights, lack of consent for marketing, and failure to cooperate with the authority. It issued a warning and a reprimand, ordered corrective measures on sales network controls and handling of rights requests, and imposed a fine of EUR 26,513,977 (5% of the statutory maximum). The decision is published on the Garante's website.

A complaint said a travel agency's online visa application form ran over an unencrypted connection and saved applicants' personal data as files on an openly accessible web server, and that the agency ignored a request to delete the complainant's data. The Ombudsman's sanctions board found breaches of the GDPR principles and of the rights and security rules, and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 6,500 on the travel agency's small group. The decision is final.

The Data Protection Ombudsman's Office examined the Motor Insurance Centre's practice of requesting full patient records from healthcare providers when handling motor injury claims, without limiting them to what was necessary. It found breaches of the data minimisation and fairness principles in Article 5(1)(a) and (c) and of data protection by design and by default in Article 25. The Ombudsman issued a reprimand and an order; the sanctions board found them insufficient and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 52,000. The Helsinki Administrative Court annulled the decisions in October 2023, and the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that annulment in March 2025.

A preventive medicine centre notified the Garante of a hacker attack in which a group obtained metadata (name, date of birth, type of radiological exam) of five patients from its PACS server and posted a partly obscured image on Twitter. The server was reachable from the internet without authentication, apparently via a router port-forwarding configuration. The Garante found the security measures inadequate and also found that the centre had not published or communicated its data protection officer's contact details. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5, 25, 32 and 37 GDPR and fined the centre EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee complained that his individualised work email accounts stayed active after his employment ended and that his deletion request went unanswered. The Garante found that Corradi s.r.l. was the controller, kept the account active until October 2019 without informing him, and ignored three requests for information from the authority. It found breaches of fairness, minimisation, storage limitation and information duties, plus failure to respond to the Garante. It imposed a EUR 20,000 fine and ordered publication of the decision.

A local health authority (ASL Latina) wrongly sent two scanned documents to an unauthorised third party in reply to an access request. One contained health data on two Covid-19 positive people, the other internal phone numbers and emails of three employees. The Garante found that disclosure lacked a legal basis and breached the integrity and confidentiality principle. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective orders because the conduct had ceased and measures were adopted.

A bank customer complained that a letter from Ubi Banca bore on the outside of the envelope the words 'credito anomalo Chieti' (anomalous credit), which could reveal his financial situation to third parties. The Garante found this breached the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and of data minimisation, contrary to its 2005 debt-recovery guidance. It imposed a fine of EUR 100,000 on the bank (now merged into Intesa Sanpaolo) and ordered publication of the decision. The bank had already replaced the wording with a code during the investigation, and this was treated as mitigating.

A UK customer complained to the UK authority that FCA Italy had not given him access to transcripts of calls with its customer service centre and to the internal case notes about his vehicle problem. The Garante, as lead authority, found that FCA failed to answer the access request within the deadline and did not give adequate reasons for withholding the data. It rejected FCA's arguments on the applicable law and on the right of defence. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered FCA to hand over the complainant's personal data in the case notes within 30 days, and fined it EUR 20,000. The Austrian authority's objection was taken into account in a revised draft decision.

A university lecturer sent his CV to Uninettuno, an online university, for a teaching appointment that was never formalised. The university then published the full CV on its website, including residential address, phone numbers, email and PEC addresses, marital status and signature, and it was indexed by search engines. After the lecturer objected, the university removed the data. The Garante found that publishing the contact and personal details breached the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, and imposed a EUR 1,000 fine plus publication of the decision on the Garante's website. The consent argument was rejected, and the rest of the CV content was archived as lawful.

A complainant asked a Finnish medical clinic for access to the complainant's patient records under Article 15 GDPR and did not receive them. The clinic was slow and passive in answering the supervisory authority and did not clearly inform patients about its role as controller. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman issued a reprimand and an order, and the sanctions board imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 for infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 12, 13, 15 and 25 GDPR.

Datatilsynet reported the municipality to the police and proposed a fine of DKK 100,000. The municipal dental service had a self-service system that, after being extended to co-parents with joint custody, let parents see the address of the resident parent and child even where name and address protection applied. Datatilsynet found the security inadequate. The Danish court imposed a fine of DKK 50,000, which the High Court upheld.

The Belgian Litigation Chamber examined a bank's information systems, notably whether they allowed data subjects to exercise their rights (rectification, diacritical signs in names), after an Inspection Service investigation. It dismissed the findings on Articles 5(1)(d), 16 and 25. It found a violation of Article 38(6) GDPR because the data protection officer held a function creating a conflict of interests (head of a department). It ordered the bank to bring the processing into compliance and imposed a fine of EUR 75,000, reduced from the EUR 100,000 initially envisaged after mitigating circumstances were considered. The Art. 30 complaint was also found not to be a violation.

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice to Northern Gas & Power Ltd, an energy broker, for making unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers registered with the TPS or CTPS, contrary to regulation 21 of PECR. The case began with a complaint from a caravan park owner about a call on 21 April 2020, and the ICO also relied on TPS and ICO complaint records. The Commissioner found a serious contravention and imposed a penalty of £75,000, reduced from £80,000 for a mitigating factor. The notice offers a 20% early payment discount.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation in November 2021 into a company, SC Nobiotic Pharma SRL. The complaint was that the company sent the complainant unsolicited commercial SMS messages without consent. The company did not answer the authority's request for information. The authority found a breach of Article 58(1) GDPR and fined the company 9,890 lei, stated as the equivalent of EUR 2,000.

The Norwegian DPA investigated Grindr after complaints from the Norwegian Consumer Council. It found that Grindr's earlier consent mechanism was not valid, because consent was not freely given. The free version of the app was conditional on consenting to data sharing with advertising partners, there was no separate consent for different purposes, and refusing meant paying for the premium version. Grindr therefore disclosed users' personal data, including GPS location and special category data, to advertising partners without a legal basis. The DPA found breaches of Articles 6(1) and 9(1) GDPR and imposed an administrative fine of NOK 65,000,000, noting several aggravating factors and one mitigating factor (the new consent mechanism).

A company, EAS, ran a credit check on a private individual who was a part-owner of a competitor, although the person had no customer or other relationship with it. EAS said it was a mistake made while using the Bisnode tool when reviewing a competitor's accounts. The Norwegian DPA found there was no legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and fined the company NOK 200,000, reduced from a notified NOK 250,000 because of the company's Covid-related fall in turnover. It also ordered the company to improve its internal controls and procedures for credit checks.

The Data Protection Commission ran an own-volition inquiry into how Limerick City and County Council used CCTV, ANPR and drones in public places. It found the Council had no lawful basis for its traffic management cameras or for sharing their live feed with the Gardaí. It also found failures on transparency (signage and an inaccessible CCTV policy) and the wrongful rejection of subject access requests. The Commissioner reprimanded the Council on several points and ordered temporary processing bans and compliance measures. She imposed administrative fines of EUR 50,000 (Article 13), EUR 25,000 (Article 12(1)) and EUR 35,000 (Article 15), EUR 110,000 in total. No fine was imposed for the Article 32(1) infringement.

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of approximately €9900 (PLN 45,000) on a public university for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to continuously ensure the confidentiality of processing activities, as well as for failing to regularly test, measure and evaluate the effectiveness of these measures.

The complainant received an unsolicited marketing letter from the defendant, which had bought his data from a third party. He asked by email and registered letter for the source of his data, objected and requested erasure, but got no reply. A first 'light' decision (69/2020) ordered compliance; the defendant again did not respond. In this decision on the merits, the Litigation Chamber found breaches of Articles 12.3, 14, 15, 17.1.c and 21.2 GDPR. It ordered the defendant to give Article 14 information to all people whose data came from the third party and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000. The complainant eventually declared himself satisfied.

Seventeen individuals complained about promotional telephone calls made on behalf of the gas supplier ZENITH by its call-centre processor One Way, to numbers listed in the Article 11 opt-out register. The cause was an employee's omission and the lack of an automated process excluding registered numbers from the call lists, over more than 1.5 million calls in the period. The Authority fined the processor EUR 30,000 for breaching Article 32(2) and (4) GDPR in conjunction with Article 28(3)(c). It reprimanded the controller ZENITH for breaching Article 28(3)(c), because its oversight and instructions were only general and insufficient.

Vastaamo, a Finnish psychotherapy provider, reported a data breach in September 2020 after an extortion letter claimed it had copied its patient database. The office found that a breach on 15.3.2019 should have been notified to the supervisory authority and to data subjects, that the breach of 20.12.2018 was not documented, and that Vastaamo had breached several other GDPR provisions on security and accountability. The Deputy Ombudsman issued a reprimand for the wider set of infringements, and the sanctions panel imposed an administrative fine of EUR 608,000 for breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 33(1) and 34(1). Vastaamo was in bankruptcy and had stopped trading, but the panel held that a fine was still effective and proportionate.
CNIL reminds controller that all processing types must be covered within the relevant privacy policy or this may constitute a breach of Article 12 GDPR and Article 13 GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA fined the company Trumf €500,185 (NOK 5,000,000) for failing to report and document repeated data breaches where people could register other people's bank account numbers to get access to their detailed purchase history.

After an investigation concluded in November 2021, the Romanian authority found that Telekom Romania Communications had collected inaccurate personal data, in particular an email address, and so sent invoices and arrears notices about another subscriber to an unrelated person who complained. It also found that the company did not act on an erasure request. Two fines were imposed, RON 24,745 (about EUR 5,000) and RON 4,949 (about EUR 1,000), together with corrective measures on data accuracy, security and handling of erasure and rectification requests.

Virgin Media Limited sent 451,217 marketing emails on 4 August 2020 to customers who had opted out of marketing, in a price-freeze email that included a reminder of their marketing preferences. After a complaint, the Information Commissioner found that the emails were direct marketing sent without valid consent, that the breach was deliberate, and that Virgin Media failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it. A monetary penalty of £50,000 was imposed under the Data Protection Act 1998 for a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR, with a 20% early-payment reduction to £40,000 available.

The complainant's representative filed a complaint with the Hungarian DPA about the respondent, a private individual who was acting as private prosecutor in criminal proceedings. The respondent emailed summonses and photos naming the complainant as a defendant to a group of company staff and to the company's central email address, on 6 January 2021 and 11 June 2021. The DPA found infringements of the principles of lawfulness, fairness and purpose limitation (Art. 5(1)(a) and (b)) and of the requirements of Art. 6(1) and Art. 9(1), and imposed a fine of HUF 300,000. The complainant's request for a fine was rejected, as the complainant is not a party on that point.

A local health authority in Parma mistakenly put two patients' diagnostic reports into an envelope addressed to a third patient and sent it by registered mail, while the third patient's own report was not enclosed. The third patient complained and the authority also notified a data breach. The Garante found the disclosure of health data unlawful, in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It fined the authority EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but imposed no corrective orders because the authority had already adopted measures.

A complaint revealed that the online traffic-fine payment portal run by Ica s.r.l. for the Municipality of Collegno let anyone view other people's fine data by entering only a predictable report number and date, because the licence-plate requirement was lost in a software update. The Garante found that Ica, as processor, had not applied adequate security measures, breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR. The pedestrian-fine aspect was treated as resolved since no personal data were involved. It imposed a fine of EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Data Protection Commission conducted an own-volition inquiry into the Teaching Council after personal data breaches involving unauthorised access to two staff email accounts. It found the Council infringed Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) by failing to apply appropriate security, and Article 33(1) by not notifying the breach without undue delay. The Council was treated as a public body, so the fine cap was EUR 1,000,000. It was fined EUR 40,000 for the security infringement and EUR 20,000 for the notification infringement, EUR 60,000 in total, and an order to bring processing into compliance and a reprimand were also imposed.

A nursing home notified a data breach after the hacker group LulzSec_ITA published radiology images on Twitter. The hackers had accessed the remote image viewer MedDream, supplied and installed by a company (the nursing home's processor), using default admin/admin credentials over unencrypted http. The Garante found that the processor's security measures (insecure network protocol and no password policy) were inadequate, breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). It imposed a fine of EUR 7,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures because the conduct had ceased to have effects.

A private clinic notified the Garante of a breach: a hacker group got into its remote radiology image viewer (MedDream) using the default admin/admin credentials over unencrypted http, and posted radiological images on Twitter. The Garante found the clinic, together with its processor, had not adopted adequate security measures (no encryption in transit, weak password practice). It treated the fault as slight negligence, noting a single isolated incident, prompt remediation and full cooperation. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the clinic EUR 30,000, with publication of the decision.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a transport company's video surveillance and on 20 March 2019 carried out an on-site visit. The restricted formation found that one camera permanently watched the receptionist and another covered a smokers' corner used by staff in their free time. Seven cameras also covered neighbouring land or the public road, which breached data minimisation. The company had also not given adequate information to data subjects under Article 13. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 6,800, which the company had accepted, and ordered no corrective measures because the company had already taken compliance steps.

A complaint was lodged with the Polish DPA against a company over the processing of the complainant's data. The President of UODO asked the company for explanations four times; one letter was received and the other three were treated as delivered after uncollected postal notices, yet the company never replied. The authority opened separate own-initiative proceedings and found breaches of Articles 31 and 58(1)(e) GDPR (lack of cooperation and no access to information). It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 18,192 (about EUR 4,000), treating the failure to provide access to information as the most serious breach under Art. 83(3).

The Belgian DPA found that a public authority infringed the GDPR by disclosing the identity of a complainant to four suspects in the context of a municipal administrative sanction procedure for illegal dumping. Since the public authority adopted measures to avoid future infringements, the Belgian DPA decided not to impose a fine.

A data subject complained that the company (called Y in the decision) asked her for a copy of her identity card when updating her personal data. The Agency found that the company had a legal obligation under the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Act to identify its client by copying an identity document, and that she had been informed under Article 13 GDPR and given a choice of how to send the copy. The request was rejected as unfounded.

The Lithuanian authority VDAI investigated UAB Prime Leasing, which runs the CityBee car rental platform, after information appeared publicly in February 2021 that customer data had been leaked. A database backup from 27 February 2018 had been left unprotected and was exposed until 16 February 2021, exposing data of 110,302 users, including personal codes, unencrypted, and passwords hashed with SHA-1. VDAI found infringements of GDPR Article 32(1)(a), (b) and (d) and imposed a fine of EUR 110,000. The company announced on 29 December 2021 that it would not appeal.

EB Associates Group Limited (EBAG), an FCA-authorised firm, paid introducers a fixed fee of £300 to £750 per referral, and those introducers made unsolicited pension-related marketing calls on its behalf. Between 11 January and 30 September 2019 these calls numbered 107,003, and the ICO found that neither EBAG nor the introducers had valid consent or an existing client relationship, contrary to regulation 21B of PECR. The Commissioner found a serious contravention, negligent but not deliberate, and imposed a penalty of £140,000, reduced by 20% to £112,000 if paid early.

Persónuvernd examined whether blood samples taken from COVID-19 patients at Landspítali in 3-7 April 2020 and sent to Íslensk erfðagreining were processed lawfully and transparently before a research addition was approved by the national research ethics committee on 7 April 2020. The samples were used for research, and consent was only collected afterwards. The authority found that the processing by Landspítali and Íslensk erfðagreining in the run-up to the research addition did not comply with the GDPR principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and of clearly specified purpose. The case was not referred to a fining procedure, so no fine was imposed.

The French DPA (CNIL) ordered Clearview AI, a company conducting facial recognition on public web sources, to stop unlawfully collecting and processing the personal data of data subjects on the French territory, delete all such personal data collected previously, and set up clearer and more efficient procedures that enable the enforcement of the right of access and right to be forgotten.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in October 2021 into Valoris Center S.R.L., a call-centre company acting as processor. A call-centre employee mistakenly attached to an email to a client of the controller an Excel file containing data of the controller's Internet Banking customers. The file exposed e-mail addresses, usernames, personal ID numbers, phone numbers, client codes and PINs of 11,169 people. The company was found to have breached Articles 29 and 32 GDPR and was fined 9,898 lei (about EUR 2,000).

The Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet) examined a breach notified by Silkeborg Municipality after a staff member emailed a list of CPR numbers, school names and school codes for 12,915 pupils to an external recipient without encryption. The municipality could not show that the email was encrypted in content, and only transport-layer encryption with TLS 1.1 was possibly used, which the authority considered inadequate. The Agency found violations of Article 32(1) GDPR and of Article 5(2) read with Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and issued a serious criticism (reprimand). No fine is stated in the text.

The Garante's newsletter reports that it fined the company that commissioned an SMS promotional campaign, as controller, for never checking that the marketing company it hired followed the contract instructions. The data came from unverified lists through a chain of subcontractors, some set up abroad without a representative in Italy. Two complainants had kept receiving unwanted messages and received no satisfactory answers. The commissioning company was fined EUR 400,000; a second company, the marketing supplier, was banned from using data from non-compliant sources and fined EUR 200,000; a third was fined EUR 90,000 for not replying to the Garante's requests.

A lawyer complained to the Garante about numerous unwanted promotional SMS sent under the Dorelan brand and about being unable to exercise his access and objection rights. The investigation showed that the brand owner B&T was the controller and Aimon, the SMS platform operator, acted as its processor. Aimon used purchased contact lists without properly verifying consent, gave evasive answers to data subjects, and sent a second SMS after the complainant had objected. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1)(a), 12 and 21 GDPR and Article 130 of the Code, banned Aimon from using personal data without verifying the lawfulness of their original collection, and fined it EUR 200,000.

The Dutch DPA fined the Minister of Finance a total of EUR 2,750,000 because the Tax Administration's Benefits department processed nationality data without a lawful basis. It kept the dual nationality of Dutch citizens in its TVS system, used nationality as an indicator in a risk-classification model for childcare benefit applications, and used nationality in detecting organised fraud. The last two processings were also unfair (discriminatory) under Article 5(1)(a). Three separate fines of EUR 750,000, 1,000,000 and 1,000,000 were imposed, with the fairness breaches taken into account in setting the amounts rather than fined separately.

A health services company notified a personal data breach: two medical reports (a blood count and an ECG without trace) of one patient were put by mistake in the envelope of another patient and handed to that person. The company said it was a single human error and pointed to its procedures and quick recovery of the documents. The Garante found the disclosure of health data had no legal basis and breached Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 6,000, ordered publication of the decision, and adopted no corrective measures because the conduct had ended.

The Norwegian Public Service Pension Fund (SPK) collected from the Tax Administration far more periodised income data than it needed for the annual settlement of disability pensions, and kept it with no deletion routine from October 2016 to October 2019. About 44,000 people were affected, and some of the data was special category data on disability pensions. SPK reported the deviation itself, but months late. Datatilsynet found breaches of data minimisation, storage limitation and the necessity requirement in Articles 6(1) and 9(2), but no breach of confidentiality. It fined SPK NOK 1,000,000, reduced from the NOK 1,500,000 announced, partly because much of the breach predated the GDPR and the case took long to handle.

Persónuvernd opened an own-initiative investigation after many tips that the government's 'Ferðagjöf' (travel gift) app demanded extensive personal data and broad access to users' phones. It found that the ministry, as controller, lacked a legal basis and valid consent, breached fairness, transparency and information duties, and failed on security and on concluding a proper processor agreement. The app developer YAY ehf. failed on data protection by design and default and on security; the app requested far-reaching phone permissions by mistake, although no data was in fact collected through them. The authority fined the ministry ISK 7,500,000 and YAY ehf. ISK 4,000,000 (less ISK 800,000 for the cost of the security audit). It ordered both to give users proper information before registration.

Persónuvernd opened an own-initiative inquiry into the government's 'Ferðagjöf' (travel gift) app, built by YAY ehf., after many tips that it demanded extensive personal data and wide access to users' phones. It found that the ministry (ANR), as controller, broke several basic data protection rules and fined it ISK 7,500,000. It found that YAY ehf. failed to ensure adequate security and data protection by design: there was no processing agreement, the app's settings were not properly configured, and the app mistakenly requested broad phone permissions and collected age and gender. YAY ehf. was fined ISK 4,000,000, less ISK 800,000 for the cost of the Syndis security audit. YAY ehf. was not fined for programming the broad access permissions, because the rules were not clear enough to cover steps that did not actually give access. Both parties were ordered to give users proper information before they register.

Persónuvernd examined, on its own initiative, the processing of personal data for SARS-CoV-2 screening and antibody testing in Iceland in 2020, carried out with Íslensk erfðagreining. It found the Chief Epidemiologist to be the controller and that the processing largely complied with the law, and it accepted the information given to data subjects at the border. It found that the processor contract between the Chief Epidemiologist and Landspítali did not fully comply with current law, and that the public information did not make clear that the antibody screening was not a research project. It ordered a compliant processor contract to be put in place, with confirmation due by 10 January 2022, and imposed no fine.

The Icelandic DPA issued a reprimand against a hospital appointed to carry out COVID-19 tests for failing to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment in violation of Article 35(1) GDPR when relocating part of their staff to another medical centre.

The Czech DPA issued a penal order (příkaz) against Společnost I., an investment firm. A former client had asked by phone in September 2019 and in writing in February, March and April 2021 for copies of his call recordings. The company never replied or explained that the recordings were no longer held, which breached the duty under Article 12(4) GDPR to inform the data subject of the reasons for not acting. The company was fined CZK 20,000, the fine being set at the lower end of the scale.

A user who was born in 2001 entered a false birth year of 1996 when opening an account in 2014 to avoid minor restrictions. After reaching adulthood he asked the service to correct his date of birth and account name; the service refused both, and he complained to the French DPA. The HBDI held that a freely chosen pseudonym cannot be inaccurate under Article 16, but that the initial refusal to correct the date of birth was improper. It issued a warning under Article 58(2)(b) and required the customer support processes to be adapted, but imposed no further sanction because the controller had already started the rectification and the complainant had caused the need for it.

The Hellenic DPA rejected a complaint by a data subject about possible automated decision-making by a bank on the grounds that there was no new evidence brought forward by the claimant. The DPA also highlighted that the data subject did not exercise their right to object under Article 21(1) GDPR.

The Swedish DPA supervised the Migration Agency's processing of personal data in the Swedish national part of the Visa Information System (VIS). It found no established breach but identified two risks: unclear status of the VIS IT architecture documentation could lead to inadequate security measures under Article 32, and the absence of a deletion routine for user logs could lead to storage longer than necessary under Article 5(1)(e). The DPA issued two warnings under Article 58(2)(a) and imposed no fine.

The Croatian DPA determined that a photograph of a person camouflaged in a jacket and wearing a protective mask did not consitute personal data according to Article 4(1) GDPR because it was impossible for the average person to identify the individual. As a result, the publication did not infringe the GDPR.

The Authority examined the Ministry of Education's use of synchronous remote teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic, delivered through the Cisco Webex platform, after complaints from teachers' unions and a parent. It found several infringements, including of Article 6 (with Article 4(5) of Law 3471/2006), Article 13 with Article 5(1)(a) and Articles 12 and 37(7), Article 25(1), Article 35(9) and Article 46. It issued reprimands for each and ordered the Ministry to bring its processing into line with the GDPR within two or four months. No fine was imposed.

The UK DPA (ICO) imposed a fine of approximately €585,739 (GBP 500,000) on the Cabinet Office for a data breach in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR. The New Years 2020 Honours List was published including postal addresses for the recipients of the Honours.

The Cypriot Commissioner announced a EUR 925,000 administrative fine on WS WiSpear Systems Ltd. The company's activities collected MAC addresses and IMSI numbers from devices during product tests and demonstrations, without the device users knowing. The Commissioner found this breached the principle of lawfulness, fairness and transparency in Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. The text says the company, in a letter, in essence admitted its responsibility, and that experts found no device monitoring or interception of private communications.

A customer complained that Komplett Bank sent him direct marketing e-mails after he had objected, that he had no opt-out when his e-mail address was registered, and that his access requests were answered late. The authority found that the marketing processing could not rely on contract as a legal basis under Article 6(1)(b), that the continued marketing after the objection breached Article 21(3), that the bank gave misleading information and no notice of the right to object (Articles 12(1), 13(1) and 21(4)), and that requests were not answered within the time limit in Article 12(3). It issued a compliance order and a reprimand, and no fine was imposed.

Vodafone Romania was sanctioned approx €2,900 for failing to implement sufficient technical and organisational measures which led to the unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data belonging to 70 natural persons.

A former employee complained that his company did not give him a copy of a written warning issued in 2017 after he asked for it. The part of the complaint about the company not telling him of the warning was dismissed, because it was an employment law question outside the Authority's scope. On the access request, the parties disagreed whether it was made orally in March 2020, so the Authority could not establish a breach of the access right. The company had sent a copy in January 2021 at the request of the complainant's union, and the complainant had therefore received it.

Two tenants of a social housing company complained that the company passed their personal data to a Dutch investigation firm as part of an asset check. The Inspection Service found several GDPR breaches, but the Litigation Chamber found that the processing took place before the GDPR applied on 25 May 2018 and did not continue afterwards. It therefore declared itself without jurisdiction ratione temporis and dismissed the complaints on a technical basis. The decision also makes general remarks on the legal basis for such checks, including Article 6(3) and Article 13(1)(c), but these are not findings of infringement.

A Belgian fitness club passed a member's personal data (name, address, date of birth, phone number, email and dates of her last visits) to a third person. That person, also a member, had wrongly paid her subscription and wanted to know whose fees he had paid. The Litigation Chamber found no valid legal basis for this further processing: it was incompatible with the original contractual purpose, and legitimate interest did not apply because the disclosure was not necessary and the member could not reasonably expect it. It found breaches of Article 5(1)(b) and Article 6 GDPR, but imposed only a reprimand, given that it was a one-off, possibly human-error incident and the club had introduced measures.

The CNPD restricted formation investigated a Luxembourg car dealership after on-site checks in March 2019 found two cameras at the workshop reception with no information notice for employees or third parties. The authority found infringements of Article 13 (information to data subjects) and Article 5(1)(c) (data minimisation). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 1,500. The two cameras were later removed, so the proposed corrective orders were not imposed.

The Finnish DPA ordered Bisnode Finland Oy to delete incorrect entries from their credit information register and change their procedure of the processing information on debtors’ ability or willingness to pay, because this was in violation of Article 25(1) GDPR.

The Finnish DPA ordered the Legal Register Centre to implement appropriate measures to ensure compliance with the GDPR by ensuring that no incorrect payment information is sent without a legal basis to credit reporting companies.

An individual asked the credit information register operator to delete four payment default entries based on court judgments, arguing that the claims were disputed and should not have been recorded. The Ombudsman found that the four entries should not have been recorded and must be corrected under the Credit Information Act. The Ombudsman also found that the controller's practice for recording court-judgment payment defaults did not comply with Article 25(1) GDPR. A reprimand was issued instead of an administrative fine, which was considered not proportionate given the role of the court data provider's practices.

Region Nordjylland notified the Danish Data Protection Agency of a security breach in the booking self-service app 'MineAftaler', which allowed logged-in users to view and delete other patients' letters and bookings by changing a number in a web request. The vulnerability was a known type of access-control flaw, existed from May 2018 to April 2021, and potentially exposed data on about 498,599 patients, including health data. The Agency found that the region had not set sufficient security requirements in its contracts with the developer and had not required adequate security-focused testing, and issued a reprimand (kritik) under Article 32(1) GDPR. No fine was imposed.

The Catalan DPA issued an opinion stating that access to document requests of administrative proceedings for environmental infringements should not include the personal data of individual polluters, except in cases of “very serious” infringements.

Coop Danmark A/S notified the Danish DPA of a personal data breach after its scanning tool found personal data, including national identification numbers, stored on a shared drive without adequate access control. The data concerned 477 employees and external consultants and dated back to 2013. The DPA issued a severe reprimand for failing to take appropriate security measures under Article 32(1) GDPR, because the company should have noticed and cleaned up the shared drive earlier. It found the breach was notified within 72 hours, so Article 33(1) was complied with.

The Office inspected a company that sells electricity and gas. From 28 July to 29 September 2021, its website listed about 50 distribution-service providers as its processors, although the data processing contracts named them as controllers and the company itself as processor. The company itself described itself as controller in that list. The Office found a breach of Article 12(1) GDPR and issued a penal order (příkaz) fining CZK 25,000, at the very bottom of the statutory range. No corrective order was made because the company removed the incorrect entries during the inspection.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation on 14 October 2021 into IKEA România SA after the company notified a personal data breach. During a children's drawing contest for IKEA Family members, the children's drawings and the participation forms, which held personal data of the children and their parents, were published on the members' online platform by mistake. The data stayed visible for about 40 hours and 114 people were affected, around half of them minors. The authority found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR and fined the company 4,948.80 lei, equal to EUR 1,000.

Romania's data protection authority finished, on 1 October 2021, an investigation into the energy producer Hidroelectrica, which began after the company sent several personal data breach notifications. It found that the company lacked adequate technical and organisational security measures, so the personal data of 325 individuals was accessed or disclosed to wrong recipients. It also found that the company kept processing the data of 3 customers after they had asked for erasure and withdrawn consent. The company received a fine of 24,739.50 lei (about EUR 5,000) for the security failure and a warning for the unlawful processing, plus corrective measures to review its security measures, train staff and keep data accurate.

The Greek DPA decided that the Athens Bar Association (ABA) was allowed to share the personal data of its members with the candidates for the elections of the ABA, as long as the further processing of these data remains compliant with the GDPR.

The CNIL restricted committee fined a French public industrial and commercial body (called X in the published text) EUR 400,000. The case concerned Excel files used to prepare promotion committees for bus drivers, which included counts of strike days per employee and absence data. The committee found breaches of data minimisation, accountability, storage limitation and security, and ordered publication of the decision. The published decision does not name the body: its name comes from the CNIL's press release (see the note below).

A complaint said a cleaning company sent customer data, including names, addresses, phone numbers, door codes and key box numbers, to its employees through WhatsApp on their personal phones. The Ombudsman found that using WhatsApp for this transfer breached the principle of integrity and confidentiality, data protection by design and by default, the controller's responsibility, and security of processing. The controller was ordered to bring its processing into line with the GDPR and was given a reprimand. No fine was imposed.

After an administrative inspection on 11 February 2020 at a bar, police found three active video cameras (two inside, one outside) with no information notice. The Garante found OTTO s.r.l., the operator, in breach of Article 13 GDPR for failing to provide information on the video surveillance. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, ordered payment within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Italian DPA fined Anfiteatro Flavio s.r.l. EUR 2,000 for operating a CCTV system at a hotel without the information notices required by Article 13 GDPR. Police inspections found the system active and no signage in place. The company did not submit any defence or documents during the procedure. The Garante also ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Luxembourg DPA (CNPD) found that the offering of a loyalty programme by a company to its customers did not amount to a regular and systematic monitoring of the customers pursuant to Article 37(1)(b) GDPR, and that the Company therefore did not need to appoint a Data Protection Officer.

The Luxembourg DPA found that a non-profit association, which belonged to a confederation of entities providing social services, had wrongfully concluded that it was obliged to appoint a DPO pursuant to Article 37(1) GDPR. However, as no violation had occurred, it closed the case.

As part of a thematic audit campaign on data protection officers, the CNPD investigated a Luxembourg bank. It found that the DPO's contact details were not published, the DPO was not involved formally and regularly in all data protection matters, the DPO's autonomy and reporting line to top management were not formally guaranteed, and the DPO's monitoring task was not shown to be adequately carried out at the start of the investigation. Remedial steps taken during the investigation did not cancel the breaches. The restricted formation imposed a single fine of EUR 18,700 and ordered the company to put a formal mechanism guaranteeing DPO autonomy in place within four months.

The CNPD opened a thematic audit campaign on the data protection officer (DPO) role in 2018, including an audit of a transport company. The investigator found failures to involve the DPO in all data protection issues, to guarantee the DPO's autonomy, and in the DPO's information/advisory and monitoring tasks. The restricted committee upheld breaches of Articles 38(1), 38(3), 39(1)(a) and 39(1)(b) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 15,400 and ordered the company to comply with Article 39(1)(b) within four months by ensuring the DPO can monitor GDPR compliance.

A customer complained that a car service dealer passed his email and vehicle data to the importer, who sent him unsolicited satisfaction surveys. The authority rejected the complaint against the dealer, but of its own motion found the importer processed the complainant's data without proper individual information or a valid legal basis. It also found the importer's general customer-satisfaction survey practice unlawful (transparency, data minimisation, legal basis, information). It fined the importer HUF 5,000,000 and ordered it to bring processing into compliance within 30 days.

The Icelandic DPA issued an injunction against a private individual to stop monitoring some shared and public areas around a multi-family house through video surveillance cameras, and to delete all the recorded material.

The ICO issued a penalty of £36,000 against Unite the Union for unsolicited direct marketing calls (in violation of Regulation 21 PECR) to 57,665 individuals who had not given informed valid consent to receive such calls.

A patient complained that a hospital website's contact and ombudsman forms were sent over an unencrypted connection, exposing health data. The Litigation Chamber found the complaint inadmissible because the complainant showed no personal interest and no processing of his data was established. The inspection's findings on Articles 24 and 32 GDPR, and on the data protection officer under Article 38, were therefore not retained for sanctions. The complaint was dismissed on technical grounds and no fine was imposed.

A member of the fitness chain Joga complained that the login password for Joga's website and app was the member's date of birth and that there was no limit on failed login attempts. Datatilsynet found that Joga had not implemented limits on failed login attempts and used members' birth dates as permanent passwords, so it had not ensured an appropriate level of security under Article 32(1) GDPR. It issued a reprimand and an order to force all members to set a sufficiently strong password at first login. No fine was imposed.
The Spanish DPA fined a controller €20,000 (reduced to €16,000) for implementing a biometric identification system without carrying out a DPIA beforehand.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation at Glove Technology SRL on 23.09.2021. It found that the company monitored employees with audio-video cameras in offices without proving a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR, and so breached the lawfulness principle of Article 5(1)(a). It fined the company 24,745 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to bring the processing into compliance, stop the audio-video processing and delete the related data records. The investigation began after a complaint about cameras recording employees and their conversations.

The Icelandic DPA dismissed a complaint relating to the publication and sharing of pictures of a teenage child on Facebook, on the ground that it was not competent to rule on whether the parties involved in this publication had exceeded the limits of their freedom of expression.

A sole trader asked the controller to let him listen to a recording of a phone call he had with it. The controller said it would provide the recording only as text, and he asked the Ombudsman to order it to provide access. The Ombudsman held that the recording contains personal data and that the applicant, as a sole trader, has a right of access under Article 15 to it. The Ombudsman found that a written transcript that matches the recording is an acceptable form, and that the controller may also offer the chance to listen to the recording. No order was made because the controller had acted in line with the GDPR requirements by providing the information in writing.

Datatilsynet opened an own-initiative case after a complaint and examined the cookie consent solutions on the website www.alstrom.dk. It found that the consent solution used until early January 2021 did not obtain valid consent, because visitors could not choose between purposes or refuse. It also criticised the redesigned consent banner from January 2021 for visually steering users towards 'ACCEPTÈR ALLE', and criticised the placing of 18 cookies before consent was given. The decision imposed serious criticism (alvorlig kritik) and no fine, citing that the error was technical and short-lived.

The State Labor Court of Baden-Württemberg held that in the letter of invitation to BEM, the names of the parties to whom health data will be disclosed must be explicitly listed and the data subject must be informed of the consent and its necessity.

A pupil complained that the school had mistakenly sent a written warning about excessive absence, including the pupil's absence rate and full name, to another pupil via e-Boks. The school did not report the incident to the Danish data protection authority, judging that a risk to the pupil was unlikely. The authority found that the school had not shown such a risk was unlikely and issued a reprimand for the failure to notify under Article 33(1). It found no basis to reject the school's assessment of its security measures under Article 32(1), so no violation was found on that point.

After a ransomware attack in January 2021 encrypted the municipality's data, deleted its backups and led to personal data being published on the dark web, Datatilsynet issued a notice of intended decision. It found that Østre Toten lacked basic security measures, including multi-factor authentication, protected backups and adequate logging, and breached Article 32 with Article 24 and the integrity and confidentiality principle in Article 5(1)(f). It proposes a fine of NOK 4,000,000 and orders the municipality to establish and document an information security management system and to carry out risk and vulnerability analyses.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €80,000 (reduced to €64,000) for allowing a third party to enter a contract with the personal data of another data subject, without their knowledge or consent, since Vodafone did not have a system in place to verify their identity.

HIV Scotland, a charity supporting people living with HIV, sent an email on 3 February 2020 to 105 members of its Community Advisory Network using the CC field instead of BCC, exposing 65 recipients' names and email addresses, from which HIV status could be inferred. The ICO found HIV Scotland failed to implement appropriate security, despite having procured MailChimp in July 2019 but not migrating this list to it. The Commissioner imposed a monetary penalty of £10,000.

The CNPD, sitting in restricted formation, decided after an audit campaign on data protection officers that a Luxembourg public body had failed to meet several DPO obligations at the start of the investigation: the DPO's contact details were hard to find on the website, the external DPO had too little involvement and resources, and there was no formalised control plan for the DPO. The body was fined EUR 18,000 and ordered to ensure the DPO has the necessary resources and to formalise the DPO's monitoring task, both within six months. Breaches of Articles 37(5) and 38(6) were not found.

A patient asked a hospital district for access to his or her health records, and the district refused to hand over the X-ray and MRI images free of charge, charging EUR 25 because the images could only be supplied on CD/DVD. The Deputy Ombudsman held that the district's duty to provide a copy of personal data free of charge also covers X-ray and MRI images given on CD or DVD. The district had not complied with Articles 12(5), 15(1) and 15(3) GDPR. No fine was imposed; the district was ordered to comply with the request and to bring its processing into line with the GDPR.

The Polish DPA fined a controller approximately €80,000 for violating Articles 33(1) and 34(1) GDPR by failing to notify the DPA after a data breach, and only providing very general information regarding the breach to data subjects.

Three individuals complained that a cosmetics seller kept phoning them for product promotion, despite objections and, for some, registration in the Article 11 opt-out register. The company claimed oral consent and that the calls were customer satisfaction checks, but produced no proof of consent or of compliance with the legitimate-interest conditions. The Authority found breaches of Article 6, Article 21 and Article 12(2) GDPR. It imposed a single fine of EUR 20,000 for all breaches.

A patient complained that two pages of her psychiatric clinical diary, kept at a mental health centre of the Sardinia health agency, were mistakenly placed in another patient's copied records and handed to that person. The Garante found that health data was disclosed without a legal basis, breaching Articles 5 and 9 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended and the agency had given assurances on organisational improvements. Mitigating circumstances included only two data subjects, a very short period, accidental human error during the Covid-19 emergency, full cooperation and prompt remedial action.

The Luxembourg DPA found that a company was in breach of its obligation to communicate the contact details of its Data Protection Officer (DPO) under Article 37(7) GDPR, and of its obligation to ensure that its DPO does not have any conflict of interests under Article 38(6) GDPR.

Dantherm was hit by a ransomware attack in 2020. Hackers used an administrator-level account that should no longer have been active, and they exfiltrated a file with data on current and former employees, which was posted on the dark web. Dantherm reported the breach to the Danish Data Protection Agency, which acted as lead supervisory authority. The agency found that Dantherm had not ensured that administrator users could not delete or alter logs and could not document when the account was active, and it issued a reprimand under Articles 32(1) and 24(1).

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone Spain €40,000 for violations of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR. The complainant received multiple invoices intended for a customer of the company and was not properly helped when they attempted to resolve this.

The CNPD ran a thematic audit campaign on data protection officers and opened an audit of a Luxembourg non-life insurance company in September 2018. The investigator alleged four failings. The restricted formation dropped the allegation on DPO qualifications because the company later showed the DPO had enough experience. It found breaches of Article 38.1 (DPO not properly involved in data protection matters) and Article 39.1.b (no adequate monitoring by the DPO at the start of the investigation). It imposed a single fine of EUR 13,200, lower than the EUR 23,400 proposed by the investigator, and declined some proposed corrective measures because the company had since taken steps.

The French DPA (CNIL) decided that the publication of its decision against the company 'Francetest' was justified given the sensitivity of the data processed and the need to ensure that all individuals concerned, as well as organisations using such services, are fully aware of the existence of persistent data security breaches.

A company operating a business-directory search platform displayed a complainant's name and his roles as managing director and shareholder of companies, data taken from the public commercial register. The complainant argued the publication lacked a justification and that he had no contract with the company. The authority held the company's legitimate interest in offering the linked register information outweighed the complainant's interests, and dismissed the complaint as unfounded.

The Polish DPA (UODO) ordered a controller to provide a data subject with information on the marketing categories attributed to them on the basis of cookies, and to indicate which information concerning them was linked to the cookie information.

The Luxembourg DPA (CNPD) imposed a fine of €5300 on a company for using a video camera surveillance system on its premises and tracking devices in some of its employees' vehicles in breach of the information obligation set out in Article 13 GDPR and in breach of the principle of data minimisation set out in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

A person who had entered ticket competitions on the controller's website kept receiving newsletters despite repeatedly trying to unsubscribe and emailing the company. The unsubscribe function had been disabled during a CMS upgrade in December 2019, and the company did not manually remove the complainant even after being told. The Authority found that the right to object to direct marketing was not honoured and that the controller lacked an organisational measure to detect this, and imposed a EUR 5,000 fine under Articles 21(3) and 25(1) GDPR.

A school employee phoned the child protection committee to report inappropriate conduct by a colleague towards pupils, without naming any child. The committee passed the report, with the complainant's personal data, to the municipality's school and leisure department, which opened an employment matter without informing him. Persónuvernd found that the committee's disclosure and the municipality's subsequent processing did not comply with the Icelandic Data Protection Act 90/2018, on grounds of lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation and data minimisation. The decision imposes no fine, reprimand or order in the text.

Two individuals complained that the company had obtained their address data (salutation, name, date of birth and address) from other address and marketing firms without their knowledge. The company said it held the data as an address publisher under the trade law rule in § 151 GewO, supported by declarations from its data suppliers that no objection had been raised. The authority dismissed the complaints as unfounded, finding that the marketing processing was lawful without explicit consent. It rejected the claims for damages because compensation claims fall to the civil courts.

The Prefecture of Genoa mistakenly published on its website a spreadsheet listing the attorneys of two companies and their adult cohabiting family members (about a hundred people), as part of anti-mafia checks. The file stayed reachable online for about seven months, even after the Prefecture removed the link, because the file's URL was still live and indexed by Google. The Garante found a breach of data minimisation and a lack of legal basis for dissemination. It fined the Prefecture EUR 11,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a company €5,000 for transferring the data of an employee without the employee's consent.

The Danish Data Protection Agency reported the Danish Cancer Society to the police and recommended a fine of DKK 800,000. The case rested on four personal data breaches (two stolen computers, two phishing attacks), all caused by the society not implementing security measures it had itself judged necessary, including multi-factor authentication after a 2018 attack. At least 1,448 people's data was compromised, in several cases including health data. The press release's update says the district court (byret) later imposed a fine of DKK 75,000.
